title: HOSA Forensic Science: Forensic Anthropology - Forensic Anthropology - Trauma
subject: Forensic Anthropology

questions.q: Injuries or bone trauma that occurred long before an individual died, characterized by smooth edges and evidence of new bone growth (callus), are categorized as:
questions.explain: Antemortem ('before death') trauma is evident by signs of healing and new bone growth (osteogenic response), meaning the individual survived the injury for an extended period.
questions.subject: Forensic Anthropology

questions.q: Trauma that occurs to bone at or near the time of death is known as perimortem trauma. Which of the following is a primary characteristic of perimortem bone fractures?
options: Significant callus formation surrounding the fracture site
Irregular, jagged breaks with contrasting discoloration
Clean, sharp fracture edges without signs of bone healing
Shrinkage and warping caused by sun bleaching
questions.explain: Because the bone is still fresh and contains organic material at the time of death, perimortem trauma usually leaves clean, sharp, or angled breaks (greenstick fractures) but shows absolutely no sign of healing (no callus).
questions.subject: Forensic Anthropology

questions.q: An anthropologist finds a skull in a wooded area. They notice damage on the temporal bone characterized by dry, brittle, jagged edges, with the inner surface of the break appearing noticeably lighter in color than the surrounding outer bone. This damage is most likely:
questions.explain: Postmortem ('after death') damage occurs when bone is dry and brittle. It tends to fracture irregularly (like dry wood). Furthermore, because the outer bone stains from soil exposure, a fresh postmortem break often reveals lighter, unstained bone underneath.
questions.subject: Forensic Anthropology

questions.q: When comparing sharp-force trauma to blunt-force trauma, which of the following characteristics is a hallmark of blunt-force trauma to the cranium?
options: A localized puncture with inward-bending margins
Radiating and concentric fracture lines extending from the point of impact
questions.explain: Blunt-force trauma disperses energy over a wide area, causing bone deformation. On the skull, it characteristically produces an impact depression, followed by radiating fractures (like a spiderweb) and concentric fracture rings.
questions.subject: Forensic Anthropology

questions.q: A skull presents with two distinct areas of blunt-force trauma, Site A and Site B. The radiating fracture lines from Site B intercept and stop at the radiating fracture lines from Site A. Applying Puppe's Rule, what can be concluded?
options: Impact A and Impact B happened exactly at the same time.
Impact A occurred prior to Impact B.
Impact B occurred prior to Impact A.
questions.explain: Puppe's Rule dictates that a later fracture will not cross a preexisting fracture line. Because the lines from Site B arrested (stopped) at the lines from Site A, Site A must have fractured first.
questions.subject: Forensic Anthropology

questions.q: A forensic analyst is interpreting gunshot (high-velocity projectile) trauma on a skull. By analyzing the beveling of the bone, they can determine the direction of the bullet. An entrance wound on the cranial vault is typically characterized by:
options: Internal beveling (smaller hole outside, larger 'crater' inside)
External beveling (larger 'crater' outside, smaller hole inside)
No beveling whatsoever, just radiating fractures
A keyhole shape consisting purely of internal beveling on all sides
questions.explain: Bullet entrance wounds to the skull typically punch a clean hole through the outer table and cause a cone-shaped 'blowout' (internal beveling) on the inner table of the skull. Exit wounds generally display external beveling.
questions.subject: Forensic Anthropology

questions.q: A 'Parry fracture' is a type of bone fracture frequently evaluated in forensic contexts to suggest the circumstances of an assault. On which bone is a Parry fracture most commonly found?
questions.explain: A Parry fracture is a defensive wound typically occurring on the shaft of the ulna. It happens when a victim raises their forearm to deflect a blow directed at the head or face.
questions.subject: Forensic Anthropology

questions.q: In forensic anthropology, trauma characterized by linear incisions, punctures, or chop marks with a V-shaped cross-section—often without the extensive radiating fractures of blunt force—is classified as:
questions.explain: Sharp-force trauma is caused by tools with a sharp edge or point, such as knives, axes, or swords. These tools leave incised wounds, V-shaped cuts in bone, or punctures, concentrating force on a very small surface area.
